title: Q3 Product Launch Planning
content: Discussed the Q3 product launch timeline with Priya and Arjun. Key milestones: MVP by July 15, beta by Aug 1, GA by Sept 10. Need to finalize the pricing model and prepare marketing collateral. Arjun suggested using AlloyDB for the analytics backend.

title: Weekly Standup Notes - March 28
content: Team standup highlights: Frontend is on track for the dashboard redesign. Sneha presented new wireframes. Backend API migration to Cloud Run is 80% complete. Rahul flagged a potential issue with the staging environment SSL certs. Action item: Rahul to fix SSL by Monday.

title: AI Agent Architecture Discussion
content: Met with the team to discuss the multi-agent architecture for SmartDesk. Decided on ADK with Gemini as the orchestrator. Sub-agents will handle email, calendar, and knowledge base queries. MCP integration for Gmail and Calendar. AlloyDB with vector search for the notes database. Deployment target: Cloud Run.

title: Client Feedback Summary - TechCorp
content: Priya shared feedback from TechCorp stakeholders. They want faster query response times on the analytics dashboard. Current P95 latency is 2.3s, target is under 500ms. Suggested migrating from standard Postgres to AlloyDB for the columnar engine. Also requested a natural language query feature for non-technical users.

title: Intern Interview Notes - Ananya Das
content: Interviewed Ananya from IIT Research Lab for the NLP intern position. Strong background in transformer models and embeddings. Published a paper on retrieval-augmented generation. Good fit for the vector search feature work. Recommendation: extend offer for Q3 internship starting July 1.

title: Weekly Standup Notes - April 4
content: Sneha finished the dashboard wireframes and moved to high-fidelity mockups. Rahul closed the staging SSL certificate issue on Monday as promised. Arjun is blocked on the pricing spreadsheet pending finance sign-off. No deploys this week due to the change freeze.

title: Weekly Standup Notes - April 11
content: Dashboard mockups approved by stakeholders. Backend API migration to Cloud Run finished at 100%. Rahul started work on the CI pipeline caching improvements. Priya raised that TechCorp is asking for a status update on the latency work.

title: Incident Postmortem - Staging SSL Expiry
content: Staging environment went down for 4 hours on March 27 when the wildcard SSL certificate expired. Root cause: the certificate was provisioned manually in 2024 and never added to the auto-renewal rotation. Rahul renewed it and migrated the cert to Certificate Manager with 30-day expiry alerts. Action item: audit all remaining manual certificates by end of April.

title: Incident Postmortem - Cloud Run Cold Starts
content: Users reported 8-12 second delays on the first request after idle periods. Root cause: Cloud Run scaled to zero and the container image was 1.8GB, so cold start pulled the full image. Fix: switched to a slim Python base image, dropping to 340MB, and set minimum instances to 1 during business hours. Cold start now averages 1.4s.

title: 1:1 with Rahul Gupta - April 2
content: Rahul wants more ownership of the deployment tooling. He is frustrated that release approvals bottleneck on a single reviewer. Agreed to give him approver rights on the staging pipeline and revisit production access next quarter. He also asked about the conference budget for KubeCon.

title: 1:1 with Sneha Reddy - April 3
content: Sneha is happy with the async working arrangement but feels disconnected from backend decisions. Agreed to invite her to the architecture review meetings. She raised that the design system has drifted: three different button components exist across the app. Action item: Sneha to write a consolidation proposal.

title: 1:1 with Arjun Mehta - April 9
content: Arjun is stretched between the pricing model work and the StartupX integration. Agreed to hand the integration to a contractor. He flagged that AlloyDB costs are higher than budgeted in the dev environment because nobody shuts instances down overnight. Action item: Arjun to set up a scheduled shutdown.

title: TechCorp Latency Follow-up Call
content: Follow-up with Priya and two TechCorp engineers on the analytics latency work. We showed the columnar engine benchmark: P95 dropped from 2.3s to 410ms on their heaviest dashboard query. They were pleased but asked whether the improvement holds at 10x data volume. Committed to running a scaled load test before the next review.

title: StartupX Integration Kickoff
content: Kickoff call with Arjun's team at StartupX. They want to embed our analytics widgets in their SaaS product. Scope: read-only API access, SSO via their identity provider, and a white-label theme. Arjun estimated six weeks. Main risk is their identity provider uses a non-standard SAML dialect.

title: Design Review - Dashboard Redesign
content: Reviewed Sneha's high-fidelity dashboard mockups. Consensus: the new filter panel is a clear improvement. Concerns raised about the density of the metrics grid on smaller laptop screens. Decision: ship the filter panel first, iterate on grid density with real user feedback. Sneha to prepare a responsive breakpoint spec.

title: Design System Consolidation Proposal
content: Sneha's proposal to consolidate the design system. Currently three button components with divergent padding, focus states, and disabled styling. Proposal: single Button primitive with variant props, migrate call sites incrementally behind a codemod. Estimated two sprints. Approved with the caveat that the codemod must be reviewed manually on the checkout flow.

title: Vector Search Index Decision
content: Debated index type for the notes vector column. Options: IVFFlat, HNSW, or no index with sequential scan. At current corpus size sequential scan is fast enough and avoids recall loss from approximate search. Decision: defer indexing until the corpus exceeds roughly 10,000 rows, then benchmark HNSW against exact search on the eval set.

title: Embedding Model Selection
content: Compared text-embedding-005 against text-embedding-004 and the multilingual variant. text-embedding-005 wins on retrieval quality for English technical text and supports output dimensionality reduction. Multilingual scored worse on our domain. Decision: text-embedding-005 at 768 dimensions. Revisit if we add non-English notes.

title: Why We Chose ADK Over a Custom Orchestrator
content: Evaluated building our own agent orchestration loop versus adopting Google ADK. Custom gives full control but we would rebuild tool calling, session state, and streaming. ADK provides sub-agent transfer and callbacks out of the box, which covers our routing needs. Downside is ADK's opinionated state model. Decision: adopt ADK, accept the constraints.

title: Interview Notes - Backend Candidate Vikram Nair
content: Interviewed Vikram for the senior backend role. Twelve years experience, mostly Java and Kotlin, recently moved to Go. Strong on distributed systems fundamentals, weaker on the data layer specifics we need. System design round went well: he caught the write amplification issue in the proposed schema unprompted. Recommendation: hire, but pair him with someone strong on Postgres.

title: Interview Notes - Frontend Candidate Meera Joshi
content: Meera interviewed for the frontend position. Excellent React and TypeScript depth. Built a design system at her previous company, which maps directly onto Sneha's consolidation work. Struggled slightly on the accessibility questions but recovered with good instincts. Recommendation: hire.

title: Ananya Internship Offer Sent
content: Sent the internship offer to Ananya Das for the Q3 NLP internship. Terms: 12 weeks starting July 1, stipend at the standard research intern band, remote with two on-site weeks. She accepted verbally on the call and will return the signed letter by Friday. Onboarding buddy: Rahul.

title: Sprint 14 Retrospective

Action items: audit manual certificates, add expiry alerting, and stop treating staging outages as low priority since they block the whole team.

title: Sprint 15 Retrospective
content: What went well: design review process is working, fewer late-stage change requests. What did not: three tickets carried over because the pricing spreadsheet blocked them. Action item: escalate cross-team blockers within 48 hours instead of waiting for standup.

title: Q2 Cloud Spend Review
content: Reviewed the Q2 cloud bill. Total 18,400 USD, up 22% quarter over quarter. Largest line items: AlloyDB at 7,200, Cloud Run at 3,100, and egress at 2,800. The AlloyDB increase is mostly the dev instance running 24/7. Decision: schedule dev instance shutdown outside business hours, projected saving 2,000 per quarter.

title: Pricing Model Discussion
content: Working session with Arjun on the SaaS pricing tiers. Proposed three tiers: Starter at 49 per seat, Growth at 99 per seat with the analytics add-on, Enterprise custom. Open question is whether to meter API calls separately or bundle a generous allowance. Finance wants gross margin above 70% at the Growth tier.

title: Pricing Model Revision After Finance Review
content: Finance rejected the first pricing proposal: Growth tier at 99 puts gross margin at 61% once inference costs are included. Revised proposal moves the analytics add-on to a paid module at 29 per seat and caps the bundled API allowance at 50,000 calls per month. Recomputed margin is 73%. Arjun to update the spreadsheet.

title: Monthly All-Hands - March
content: Company update: revenue tracking 8% ahead of plan, two new enterprise logos signed. Engineering shipped the Cloud Run migration. Product previewed the dashboard redesign. Open question from the floor about the hiring freeze, answered: the freeze applies to non-engineering roles only through Q2.

title: Monthly All-Hands - April
content: Company update: revenue still ahead of plan but new logo acquisition slowed. Engineering demoed SmartDesk to the whole company and it landed well. Announced Ananya joining as an NLP intern in July. Reminder that the office will be closed for the long weekend in early May.

title: Vendor Evaluation - Observability Platforms
content: Compared Datadog, Grafana Cloud, and staying on Cloud Monitoring. Datadog has the best out-of-box experience but pricing scales badly with our container count. Grafana Cloud is cheaper and we already use Prometheus exporters. Cloud Monitoring is free-ish but weak on trace correlation. Leaning Grafana Cloud, pending a two-week trial.

title: Observability Trial Results
content: Two-week Grafana Cloud trial concluded. Ingest worked cleanly with the existing Prometheus exporters. Trace correlation is adequate though the UI is slower than Datadog. Cost estimate at our volume is 640 per month versus Datadog's 2,100. Decision: adopt Grafana Cloud, migrate dashboards over the next sprint.

title: Security Review - OAuth Token Storage
content: Reviewed how SmartDesk stores Google OAuth tokens. Currently tokens are written to a local JSON file on the Cloud Run instance, which is ephemeral and not encrypted at rest beyond the platform default. Risk: tokens are readable by anything in the container. Recommendation: move to Secret Manager with per-user keys, or encrypt with a KMS key before writing.

title: Dependency Audit - April
content: Ran the dependency audit across all services. Three high-severity findings, all in transitive dependencies of the older API service. Two are patched by upgrading the HTTP client library. The third has no fix available; mitigated by disabling the affected XML parsing path, which we do not use. No findings in the SmartDesk agent dependencies.

title: Google Cloud Summit Notes
content: Attended the Google Cloud Summit. Key sessions: AlloyDB columnar engine deep dive, and a talk on agent orchestration patterns. Met Priya Sharma from TechCorp at the AI/ML partnerships booth, which started the current engagement. Picked up that AlloyDB now supports in-database embedding generation, which simplifies our ingestion path.

title: KubeCon Trip Report
content: Rahul attended KubeCon on the conference budget. Most useful sessions were on progressive delivery and on cutting container image size. He brought back the slim base image idea that later fixed our cold start problem. Less useful: the service mesh track, which assumed a scale well beyond ours.

title: Q3 Roadmap Draft
content: Draft Q3 roadmap. Committed: GA launch, StartupX integration, design system consolidation. Stretch: natural language query for TechCorp, and vector search quality improvements. Explicitly out of scope: mobile app, multi-region deployment. Capacity assumes Ananya joins in July and Vikram starts in June.

title: Launch Readiness Checklist Review
content: Walked the GA launch readiness checklist. Green: load testing, runbooks, on-call rotation. Amber: documentation, which is roughly 60% complete. Red: the pricing page, blocked on the finance-approved tiers. Decision: documentation can land the week of launch, but the pricing page is a hard blocker.

title: Weekly Standup Notes - April 18
content: Vikram accepted the backend offer and starts June 2. Sneha began the button consolidation codemod. Rahul migrated the first set of dashboards to Grafana Cloud. Blocked: the scaled load test for TechCorp is waiting on a data generation script.

title: Weekly Standup Notes - April 25
content: Load test data generation script finished, test scheduled for next week. Grafana migration is half done. Documentation push started for the GA launch. Arjun reported the AlloyDB dev shutdown schedule is live and the first week showed the expected saving.

title: TechCorp Scaled Load Test Results
content: Ran the scaled load test at 10x data volume for TechCorp. P95 held at 680ms, well inside their 2 second ceiling but above the 500ms target measured at 1x. Bottleneck is the join against the dimension tables, not the columnar scan. Recommendation to TechCorp: denormalise two dimension tables, which projects P95 back under 500ms.

title: TechCorp Natural Language Query Scoping
content: Scoped the natural language query feature TechCorp asked for. Approach: translate a question to SQL with Gemini, validate the generated SQL against an allowlist of tables and columns, then execute read-only. Main risks are hallucinated columns and expensive queries. Mitigation: schema-constrained prompting plus a query cost estimate check before execution.

title: Chunking Strategy Notes
content: Notes on document chunking for retrieval. Whole-document embedding fails once a document covers several topics because one vector must represent all of them. Fixed-size chunking splits mid-sentence and hurts readability of citations. Sentence-aligned chunks with token overlap are the usual compromise. Overlap costs storage roughly proportional to the overlap fraction.

title: Reranking Approaches Survey
content: Survey of reranking approaches. Cross-encoders score query and document jointly and are far more accurate than bi-encoder similarity, but cost one model call per candidate. Lexical rerankers like BM25 are nearly free and complement dense retrieval on rare terms. Reciprocal rank fusion combines rankings without needing score calibration. LLM rerankers are the most accurate and the most expensive.

title: Architecture Review - April 16
content: Sneha joined her first architecture review. Agenda: vector index decision, OAuth token storage, and the natural language query design. Deferred the index decision pending corpus growth. Approved moving OAuth tokens to Secret Manager. Natural language query design needs another pass on the SQL validation layer.

title: 1:1 with Priya Sharma - April 22
content: Priya is our main TechCorp contact and increasingly acts as their internal champion. She warned that a competing vendor is pitching their analytics team. Her advice: get the scaled load test results in front of their CTO quickly. She also asked whether we would consider a co-marketing case study after GA.

title: On-Call Rotation Setup
content: Set up the on-call rotation ahead of GA. Four engineers, one week each, primary and secondary. Escalation path goes primary, secondary, then engineering lead. Paging only for customer-facing outages and data loss risk; everything else waits for business hours. Runbooks live in the ops repo and each must be tested once before GA.

title: Code Review Guidelines
content: Agreed code review guidelines. Reviews should complete within one business day. Reviewers focus on correctness, then clarity, then style, and style comments should be non-blocking. Any comment that blocks a merge must say what would unblock it. Large refactors need a design note before the pull request, not after.

title: Change Freeze Policy
content: Defined the change freeze policy. Freezes apply the week before a major launch and over company holidays. During a freeze only fixes for customer-facing incidents ship, and they need a second approver. The March freeze blocked several deploys and delayed the dashboard work, so freezes will now be announced two weeks ahead.

title: Incident Postmortem - Duplicate Agent Responses
content: Users saw SmartDesk answer the same question twice. Root cause: after a sub-agent completed, control returned to the root agent, which reprocessed the original prompt. The ADK loop does not terminate on a null response. Fix: a before-model callback sets a transferred flag and returns an empty text response, which ends the turn. Regression test added.

title: Incident Postmortem - Embedding Dimension Mismatch
content: Ingestion failed for a batch of notes with a dimension mismatch error. Root cause: a developer tested with a 384-dimension local model and left the environment variable set, then ran ingestion against the shared database where the column is 768. No data was corrupted because the insert failed atomically. Fix: assert the embedder dimension matches the column before any write.

title: DesignHub Collaboration Notes
content: Working session with Sneha at DesignHub on the shared component library. They want to consume our design tokens directly rather than copying values. Agreed to publish tokens as a versioned package. Sneha prefers async review over live calls, so we will use recorded walkthroughs plus written feedback.

title: Weekly Standup Notes - May 2
content: Grafana dashboard migration complete. Documentation at 80% for GA. Sneha's codemod landed for the button primitive, checkout flow reviewed manually as agreed. Rahul is testing runbooks one by one. Blocked: pricing page still waiting on final tier approval.

title: Weekly Standup Notes - May 9
content: Pricing tiers approved by finance, pricing page unblocked and in progress. Vikram's onboarding plan drafted ahead of his June start. Load test results shared with TechCorp. No incidents this week.

title: Runbook Testing Results
content: Tested all six GA runbooks in a game day exercise. Four passed cleanly. The database failover runbook had stale connection string instructions from before the Cloud Run migration. The rollback runbook assumed a deployment tool we no longer use. Both rewritten and retested. Lesson: runbooks rot silently and need testing on a schedule, not once.

title: Secret Manager Migration
content: Migrated OAuth token storage from local JSON files to Secret Manager as the security review recommended. Each user's refresh token is stored under a per-user secret name with the service account granted accessor only on its own prefix. Local development still uses file storage behind a flag, which is documented as development-only.

title: Session State and Multi-User Isolation
content: Reviewed how SmartDesk isolates state between users. ADK session state is keyed per session, but our OAuth layer originally used a single process-wide token file, meaning a second user on the same instance could inherit the first user's credentials. Fixed alongside the Secret Manager migration by keying tokens to the session user. This was the most serious bug found so far.

title: Contractor Selection for StartupX Integration
content: Reviewed three contractors for the StartupX integration work Arjun handed off. Selected the one with prior SAML integration experience, since the non-standard SAML dialect is the main project risk. Rate is 85 per hour, estimated 180 hours. Contract includes a knowledge transfer session before handover.

title: StartupX SAML Integration Problems
content: The StartupX identity provider sends assertions with an unsigned response wrapper and a signed assertion, which our library rejects by default. Contractor confirmed this is legal per spec but unusual. Options: relax validation for this tenant only, or ask StartupX to reconfigure. Chose to ask StartupX first, since relaxing signature validation per tenant is a security footgun.

title: StartupX SAML Resolution
content: StartupX agreed to reconfigure their identity provider to sign the full response. Integration testing passed after the change. No per-tenant validation exceptions needed, so the security posture stays clean. Integration is now two weeks ahead of the six week estimate.

title: Responsive Breakpoint Spec
content: Sneha delivered the responsive breakpoint spec for the metrics grid. Three breakpoints: four columns above 1440px, two columns between 1024 and 1440, single column below. Metric cards reflow rather than shrink, since shrinking made the sparklines unreadable. Approved without changes.

title: Accessibility Audit - Dashboard
content: Ran an accessibility audit on the redesigned dashboard. Colour contrast passes AA throughout. Keyboard navigation works but the filter panel traps focus when opened. Screen reader announces metric values without their units. Two fixes assigned to Meera as her first task after joining.

title: Meera Joshi Offer and Start Date
content: Meera accepted the frontend offer, starting May 20. She negotiated a slightly higher band, approved given her design system experience directly serves the consolidation work. Onboarding buddy is Sneha, which also gives Sneha the mentorship exposure she asked for in our 1:1.

title: Onboarding Plan Template
content: Wrote a standard onboarding plan template after realising Vikram and Meera were both getting ad hoc treatment. Week one is environment setup and reading. Week two is a small scoped bug fix shipped to production. Weeks three and four are a feature with a buddy reviewing. Buddy assignment is mandatory, not optional.

title: Q3 Budget Request
content: Submitted the Q3 budget request. Headcount covers Vikram and Meera as already approved plus the contractor. Cloud spend projected at 21,000 for the quarter, up from 18,400, driven by GA traffic rather than waste. Conference budget requested for two people. Tooling adds Grafana Cloud at 640 per month and drops the unused load testing licence.

title: Monthly All-Hands - May
content: Company update: GA launch date confirmed for September 10. Meera introduced to the company. Engineering highlighted the StartupX integration running ahead of schedule. Question from the floor about on-call compensation, answered: on-call weeks carry a stipend starting with the GA rotation.

title: Sprint 16 Retrospective
content: What went well: the game day exercise found two broken runbooks before they mattered. What did not: the pricing page blocked for three weeks on a decision that took one meeting to make once escalated. Action item: any blocker older than one week goes on the all-hands agenda automatically.

title: Sprint 17 Retrospective
content: What went well: onboarding template made Meera's first week noticeably smoother than Vikram's will be if we do nothing. What did not: two production deploys required manual database steps that were not in the runbook. Action item: no deploy ships with manual steps unless they are written down and reviewed.

title: Read Replica Evaluation
content: Evaluated adding an AlloyDB read replica for analytics queries. Benefit: isolates heavy dashboard scans from transactional writes. Cost: roughly 2,400 per quarter. At current load the primary handles both comfortably, and the columnar engine already absorbed the worst queries. Decision: revisit after GA traffic data, do not provision now.

title: Caching Layer Discussion
content: Discussed adding a cache in front of the analytics API. Most dashboard queries repeat within a five minute window, so a short TTL cache would cut load meaningfully. Concern is stale data on dashboards users expect to be live. Compromise: cache with a 60 second TTL and an explicit refresh control in the UI.

title: Penetration Test Scope
content: Agreed scope for the pre-GA penetration test. In scope: the public API, the SmartDesk agent endpoints, the OAuth flow, and the tenant isolation boundary. Out of scope: physical security and social engineering. Test window is the last week of July, deliberately before the change freeze so findings can be fixed.

title: TechCorp Denormalisation Follow-up
content: TechCorp implemented the dimension table denormalisation we recommended. Their P95 at 10x volume dropped to 430ms, back inside the 500ms target. Their CTO joined the call to say this was the deciding factor against the competing vendor Priya warned about. Case study conversation reopened.

title: TechCorp Case Study Agreement
content: TechCorp agreed to a co-marketing case study after GA. They will allow named attribution and the latency numbers, but not the data volumes or their internal schema details. Marketing to draft, Priya reviews internally before publication. Target publication is four weeks after GA.

title: Documentation Structure Decision
content: Decided how to structure the product documentation before the GA push. Four sections: getting started, guides by task, API reference generated from the OpenAPI spec, and operations. The generated reference removes the drift problem we had when reference docs were written by hand. Guides stay hand-written because generated ones read badly.

title: Talk Proposal - Agent Architecture
content: Drafted a conference talk proposal on the SmartDesk multi-agent architecture. Angle: what breaks when you compose agents, using the duplicate response bug and the multi-user token leak as concrete examples. Both are the kind of failure people hit and do not write about. Submitted to two conferences.

title: 1:1 with Sneha Reddy - May 14
content: Sneha is enjoying the architecture reviews and says the context makes her design decisions better. She is nervous about mentoring Meera since she has not onboarded anyone before. Walked through the onboarding template together. She raised that design work is still being requested through direct messages rather than tickets.

title: 1:1 with Rahul Gupta - May 16
content: Rahul is happier with staging approver rights and wants to know the criteria for production access. Agreed on concrete criteria: six months tenure, two incidents handled as primary on-call, and a completed runbook review. He met two of three already. He asked to attend KubeCon again next year.

title: Design Request Intake Process
content: Fixed the problem Sneha raised about design work arriving through direct messages. All design requests now go through a single intake form that captures the goal, the deadline, and who the decision maker is. Sneha triages weekly. Direct messages get redirected to the form rather than answered, which is the only way this sticks.

title: Incident Postmortem - Grafana Alert Storm
content: The Grafana migration produced an alert storm: 340 pages in twenty minutes at 2am. Root cause: the migrated alert rules used the old Prometheus label schema, so every rule evaluated as firing. Nobody was harmed because the rules were still routed to a test channel. Lesson: migrate alert rules to a test route first, always, which is exactly what saved us here.

title: Incident Postmortem - Vector Search Returning Nothing
content: SmartDesk began returning no results for every notes search. Root cause: a failed migration left the content_embedding column populated with nulls for rows inserted during the window, and the ORDER BY pushed nulls last but the LIMIT 5 was consumed by them. Fix: backfilled embeddings and added a NOT NULL filter to the retrieval query. Detected by a user, not by monitoring, which is the real finding.

title: Evaluation Before Optimisation
content: Argued in the architecture review that we should not tune retrieval further until we can measure it. Currently nobody can say whether search_notes is good, because there is no labelled set and no metric. Proposal: build a small labelled question set and measure recall and MRR before changing chunking or adding a reranker. Approved as the next piece of work.

title: GA Launch Communication Plan
content: Planned the GA launch communications. Blog post on launch day, email to the waitlist the morning of, and a social thread. Customer-facing changelog entry goes out the same hour. Support gets a briefing document two days early with the top ten expected questions. No press outreach, since the audience is developers who ignore it.

title: Post-GA Priorities Draft
content: Draft of what comes after GA. Highest value is the natural language query feature, since two customers have now asked. Second is retrieval quality work on the notes search. Third is the mobile-responsive pass. Explicitly deprioritised: multi-region, which nobody has asked for and which would consume the whole quarter.

title: Architecture Review - May 21
content: Agenda: caching layer TTL, read replica decision, and the retrieval evaluation proposal. Approved the 60 second cache TTL with a manual refresh control. Deferred the read replica pending GA traffic. Approved building the retrieval eval harness before any retrieval changes, which was the main outcome.

title: Load Testing Tool Replacement
content: The paid load testing licence expires in June and costs 3,200 per year. We used it twice. Evaluated k6 as a replacement, which is open source and scripts in JavaScript. Reproduced the TechCorp scaled load test in k6 with results within 4% of the paid tool. Decision: drop the licence, use k6.

title: Cost of Inference Analysis
content: Analysed per-request inference cost for SmartDesk. Average conversation makes 3.2 model calls at roughly 1,800 input tokens and 400 output tokens each. At Gemini 2.5 Flash pricing this is well under a cent per conversation. Embedding costs are negligible since notes are embedded once on write. The cost risk is not the model, it is unbounded agent loops, which the callback guard now prevents.

title: Vikram Nair First Week
content: Vikram started June 2. Week one followed the onboarding template: environment setup, architecture reading, and shadowing an architecture review. He immediately questioned why the notes table has no index on created_at, which is a fair catch. Paired with Rahul on Postgres specifics as the interview recommended.

title: Meera Joshi First Month
content: Meera shipped the two accessibility fixes in week two as planned. She then took the focus trap fix further and audited every modal in the app, finding four more instances. Sneha reports the mentoring is going well and says having to explain decisions improved her own clarity. Meera asked about the design system versioning strategy.

title: Design Token Package Versioning
content: Decided the versioning strategy for the design token package DesignHub will consume. Semantic versioning, with token removals treated as breaking changes and requiring a major bump. Token additions are minor. Value changes are the hard case: a colour shifting slightly is technically breaking for anyone matching exact values, but treating it as major would make releases impossible. Decision: value changes are minor, documented in the changelog prominently.

title: Penetration Test Findings
content: Penetration test completed. Two medium findings and four low. Medium one: the API returns different error messages for a non-existent tenant versus an unauthorised one, allowing tenant enumeration. Medium two: session tokens do not rotate after privilege change. Both fixed within the week. No high or critical findings, which is a good result before GA.

title: Deploy Automation Improvements
content: Removed the manual database steps from the deploy process that sprint 17 flagged. Migrations now run as a pre-deploy job with an explicit approval gate for anything destructive. Rollback is a single command. Tested in staging four times before trusting it in production.

title: Weekly Standup Notes - June 6
content: Vikram finished week one onboarding. Penetration test findings both fixed. Documentation reached 95%. k6 load tests running in CI nightly now. Blocked: nothing this week, first time in two months.

title: Weekly Standup Notes - June 13
content: Vikram shipped his first production change, an index on notes.created_at. Meera's modal accessibility work merged. Cache layer with 60 second TTL deployed behind a flag. Preparing for the July penetration test retest.

title: Index on notes.created_at
content: Vikram added the missing index on notes.created_at. Queries listing recent notes were doing a sequential scan and sort. At current row counts the impact is small, but the fix is cheap and the query pattern only grows. Benchmark before: 34ms. After: 2ms. Good first change.

title: Sprint 18 Retrospective
content: What went well: zero blockers for the first time in two months, and the deploy automation removed a whole class of manual error. What did not: the cache flag was left off for a week because nobody owned turning it on. Action item: feature flags get an owner and a target enable date when created.

title: New Prospect - Meridian Analytics
content: Intro call with Meridian Analytics, referred by Priya at TechCorp. They have a similar analytics latency problem but at roughly triple the data volume. Interested in the columnar engine story. Concern raised about our company size and support guarantees, which is the usual objection at this stage. Next step: technical deep dive with their platform team.

title: Meridian Technical Deep Dive
content: Technical deep dive with Meridian's platform team. They pushed hard on multi-region, which we do not support and have deprioritised. Their data residency requirements make this a real blocker rather than a preference. Honest answer given: we cannot serve this in the next two quarters. They appreciated the directness and asked to stay in touch.

title: Multi-Region Reconsideration
content: Meridian's data residency requirement reopened the multi-region question we deprioritised. One lost deal does not justify a quarter of work. But if data residency appears in the next two enterprise conversations, the calculus changes. Decision: no work now, but track residency as an explicit reason-lost field in the pipeline so we have data next quarter.

title: Talk Proposal Accepted
content: The agent architecture talk was accepted at one of the two conferences. Slot is 30 minutes in the AI engineering track, in October. Content plan: the duplicate response bug, the multi-user token leak, and the retrieval evaluation work, assuming it produces numbers worth showing by then. Rahul offered to help rehearse.

title: Monthly All-Hands - June
content: Company update: GA on track for September 10. Penetration test passed with no critical findings. Meridian deal lost on multi-region, explained openly rather than buried. Vikram and Meera both introduced. Question about whether the September date could slip, answered: the only hard blocker left is documentation and it is at 95%.

title: Feature Flag Ownership Policy
content: New policy after the cache flag sat off for a week. Every feature flag gets an owner and a target enable date at creation time. Flags past their target date appear in a weekly report. Flags older than 90 days must be either removed or promoted to permanent configuration, because stale flags are how code paths rot untested.

title: Engineering Offsite - Day One Notes
content: Full day of sessions at the engineering offsite. Morning opened with a review of the year so far. Revenue is ahead of plan and the GA date has held through three months of planning, which is unusual for us and worth noting. The Cloud Run migration was called out as the single largest reliability improvement, having removed an entire class of instance management problems. Second session covered the incident history. We had five notable incidents: the staging SSL expiry, Cloud Run cold starts, duplicate agent responses, the Grafana alert storm, and the vector search returning nothing. The pattern across all five is that four of them were detected by a human rather than by monitoring. Consensus was that our alerting covers infrastructure well and product behaviour badly. Action item: define product-level health checks that exercise a real user path, including a notes search that asserts non-empty results. Third session was on the retrieval quality problem. Nobody in the room could state whether SmartDesk's notes search was good, which several people found uncomfortable given it is the core of the product's knowledge features. The proposal to build a labelled evaluation set before touching retrieval was restated and had broad support. Discussion covered what to measure: recall at k as the primary metric since the agent consumes several results, and mean reciprocal rank as a secondary since the top result disproportionately shapes the model's answer. Afternoon covered hiring and team shape. Vikram and Meera have both landed well, and the onboarding template is the reason. Sneha's mentoring of Meera came up as a success worth repeating. Open question about whether the team needs a dedicated data engineer or whether the current split works; deferred to Q4 planning. Final session was an open floor. Topics raised: on-call compensation, which is now settled; the design intake process, which people report is working; and a request for more architecture reviews, since the ones we hold are considered valuable but too infrequent. Agreed to move architecture reviews from monthly to fortnightly.

title: Engineering Offsite - Day Two Notes
content: Day two was working sessions rather than presentations. First session was a deep dive on the retrieval pipeline as it stands today. The current implementation embeds each note whole with text-embedding-005, stores a 768 dimension vector, and retrieves with cosine distance and a hard-coded limit of five. There is no chunking, no reranking, and no evaluation. The group walked through the failure modes this implies. Whole-note embedding means a note covering several topics gets one vector that sits between all of them and close to none, so a specific question about one topic in a long note may not retrieve it. A fixed limit of five with no reranking means the fifth-best vector match is presented with the same confidence as the first. And without evaluation, any change to any of this is a guess. Second session designed the evaluation harness. Decided on roughly thirty questions mapped to the notes that genuinely answer them, with the explicit caveat that generated labels must be reviewed by a human before they are trusted, because a label set produced by the same class of model being evaluated will flatter it. Metrics agreed as recall at one, three, five, and ten, plus mean reciprocal rank at the same cutoffs. Third session covered chunking. Consensus that chunking should be token-based with configurable size and overlap, sentence-aligned so citations read well, and that chunks must link back to the parent note so the agent can cite something a user recognises. Someone raised that our notes are mostly short and chunking may therefore show no improvement at all, and that this result should be reported honestly rather than buried. Fourth session covered reranking. Options discussed were lexical scoring, reciprocal rank fusion, a cross-encoder, and using Gemini as a reranker directly. The tradeoff is accuracy against latency and cost, and the group wanted real measured numbers rather than the usual assertions. Closing discussion was about what makes this work worth doing at all. The argument that landed was that retrieval quality is currently an article of faith, and faith is not a property you can improve deliberately.

title: Half-Year Engineering Review
content: Written half-year review covering January through June. Delivery: the Cloud Run migration completed without customer-visible downtime, the dashboard redesign shipped, the StartupX integration landed two weeks early, and the design system consolidation is complete. GA remains on track for September 10, which is the same date committed in March. Reliability: five notable incidents, none causing data loss, and the longest customer-visible impact was under an hour. The staging SSL expiry consumed four hours of team time and was entirely preventable. Cold starts affected real users for roughly two weeks before the slim image fix. The most serious issue by severity was the multi-user OAuth token leak, which could have exposed one user's mailbox access to another user on the same instance; it was found internally during a security review rather than by a customer, and fixed alongside the Secret Manager migration. Cost: quarterly cloud spend rose from 15,100 to 18,400 and is projected at 21,000 for Q3. The rise is dominated by GA preparation traffic rather than waste, though the AlloyDB development instance running around the clock was genuine waste and is now on a shutdown schedule saving roughly 2,000 per quarter. Dropping the load testing licence saves a further 3,200 per year with no capability lost. Team: two hires, Vikram on backend and Meera on frontend, both onboarded through the new template and both productive inside a month. One intern, Ananya, starting July. Sneha took on mentoring for the first time and it went well. Rahul gained staging approver rights and is close to meeting the production access criteria. Open risks going into the second half: documentation is the only remaining hard blocker for GA; multi-region remains unsupported and has already cost one deal; and retrieval quality in the knowledge base features is unmeasured, meaning we cannot tell whether it is a strength or a liability. That last item is the one most likely to be a surprise, because unlike the others nobody currently knows the answer.

title: Q3 Planning Session - Full Notes
content: Full-day Q3 planning. Opened with capacity. The team is seven engineers plus one intern and one contractor. GA consumes roughly 40% of capacity through September, which is more than the 25% originally assumed, mainly documentation and launch readiness work. Committed items. GA launch on September 10, non-negotiable date. StartupX integration completion including knowledge transfer from the contractor. Design system consolidation, already largely done. Penetration test remediation, which turned out to be small. Natural language query feature for TechCorp, scoped at four weeks with the SQL validation layer as the risky part. Stretch items. Retrieval quality improvements to the notes search, contingent on the evaluation harness existing first so improvements can be demonstrated rather than asserted. The caching layer promotion from flag to default. A mobile-responsive pass on the dashboard. Explicitly out of scope. Multi-region deployment, despite the Meridian loss, on the reasoning that one lost deal does not justify a quarter of work. Mobile applications. Any work on the older API service beyond security patching. Risks discussed. Documentation is the single hard blocker for GA and sits at 95%, which historically is where documentation stalls. The natural language query feature has a real failure mode where generated SQL is expensive rather than wrong, and a cost estimate check is the mitigation. Ananya's internship overlaps GA, so her project must not sit on the critical path; assigned her to the retrieval evaluation work, which is valuable but not launch-blocking. Dependencies. The pricing page depends on finance, which has historically been the slowest dependency and caused a three-week block last quarter. Escalation path agreed in advance this time. Closing decision was to hold the September 10 date and cut stretch items rather than move it, since the date has been communicated to customers including TechCorp and Meridian.

title: SmartDesk Product Review - Knowledge Features
content: Deep review of SmartDesk's knowledge base features specifically, separate from the email and calendar integrations. Current capabilities. Semantic search over meeting notes using vector similarity. Contact lookup by name, email, or company using simple pattern matching. Task listing, creation, and status updates. Note creation with automatic embedding generation on write. What works well. Contact lookup is reliable because it is exact pattern matching over a small table and users describe it as predictable. Task management is heavily used and the update flow works. Note creation is frictionless. What works poorly or is unknown. Notes search is the weak point, and more precisely it is the unknown point. Users occasionally report that a note they know exists does not surface, but we have no systematic measurement, so we cannot distinguish a retrieval problem from a phrasing problem from a user expectation problem. The hard-coded limit of five results means a query matching six relevant notes silently drops one, with no signal to the user or the agent that this happened. There is no chunking, so a long note covering several topics is represented by a single averaged vector. There is no reranking, so the ordering the vector index produces is the ordering the agent sees. Specific user complaints collected. One user searched for the SSL certificate incident and got the standup note mentioning SSL rather than the postmortem, which is arguably correct by similarity and wrong by intent. Another searched for pricing and got the original proposal rather than the revised one, which is a recency problem rather than a relevance problem. Both suggest that pure cosine similarity on whole notes is insufficient. Recommendation. Build measurement before building improvements. Without a labelled set and a metric, every change to this pipeline is an opinion.

title: Incident Postmortem - GA Launch Day Traffic
content: Detailed postmortem of GA launch day. Timeline. Blog post published at 09:00. Traffic rose steadily through the morning, peaking at roughly 14 times baseline around 13:00. First alert fired at 13:07 for elevated API latency. P95 reached 3.1 seconds against a 500 millisecond target. No requests failed outright and no data was lost. Latency recovered to normal by 14:20 after intervention. Root cause. Three compounding factors. The cache layer was deployed behind a flag and the flag was on, but its 60 second TTL meant the cold cache at the traffic ramp provided little protection during the steepest climb. Cloud Run minimum instances were set to one for business hours, sized against pre-launch traffic, so autoscaling had to react from a near-cold state. And the analytics dimension table join, the same bottleneck identified in the TechCorp load test, degraded non-linearly under concurrency in a way the load test at steady state had not revealed. Intervention. Raised minimum instances to eight, which absorbed the autoscaling lag within four minutes. Increased cache TTL to 300 seconds temporarily. Both changes were reverted to tuned values two days later once traffic stabilised. What went well. Alerting fired within seven minutes and the on-call rotation worked exactly as designed; the primary acknowledged in two minutes and did not need to escalate. The runbook for scaling Cloud Run was accurate, having been tested in the game day exercise. No customer reported the slowdown before we detected it, which is the first incident of the year where that is true. What went badly. The load test measured steady state, not a ramp, and the difference is precisely where the failure lived. Capacity settings were sized for the traffic we had rather than the traffic a launch produces, which in hindsight is an obvious mistake. Action items. Load tests must include a ramp profile, not only steady state. Capacity settings get an explicit review before any announced event. Investigate the dimension join concurrency behaviour, which is a real bug rather than a tuning problem.

title: Retrieval Pipeline Design Document
content: Design document for the improved retrieval pipeline. Problem statement. SmartDesk's notes search is unmeasured. The current implementation embeds notes whole, retrieves the five nearest by cosine distance, and returns them. Whether this is good is unknown, and therefore whether any change improves it is also unknown. Goals. Make retrieval quality measurable with a labelled set and standard metrics. Improve recall on long multi-topic documents. Improve the ordering of results so the top result is more often the right one. Keep the pipeline portable between AlloyDB and Postgres with pgvector so development does not require a running cloud database. Non-goals. Replacing the embedding model. Adding a vector index, which is premature at current corpus size. Supporting non-English notes. Introducing a retrieval framework, since the stack is deliberately ADK plus plain SQL and the mechanics should stay legible. Proposed design, in three stages, each measured against the previous. Stage one is the evaluation harness itself: a labelled question set, recall at k and mean reciprocal rank at several cutoffs, and a committed baseline for the current implementation. Nothing changes in the pipeline at this stage, which is the point. Stage two is chunking. Token-based with configurable size and overlap, sentence-aligned, chunks linked to parent notes by foreign key so citations resolve to something the user recognises. A separate chunks table, additive, leaving the notes table and its embedding column untouched so the baseline path keeps working. Expectation is that this helps on long notes and does nothing on short ones, and the honest reporting of a null result on short notes is part of the deliverable. Stage three is reranking. Retrieve a wider candidate set, somewhere between twenty and thirty, then rerank down to five. At least two rerankers compared: something cheap and lexical, and something LLM-based using Gemini as a cross-encoder. The comparison must report accuracy, latency, and cost together, because a reranker that adds three seconds of latency to save one position of rank is not obviously worth it. Open questions. Whether the labelled set should be generated from the notes themselves, which risks the questions being phrased too much like the source text and inflating scores. Whether recall or MRR should be the headline metric given the agent consumes five results but weights the first most heavily.

title: Year-End Technical Debt Register
content: Consolidated register of known technical debt with an honest assessment of each. The older API service. Still running, still on the deprecated HTTP client, still carrying one unfixable transitive vulnerability mitigated by disabling an unused code path. Nobody wants to own it. Cost of leaving it: one security finding per audit and a growing gap from the main stack. Cost of fixing: roughly six weeks. Verdict: leave it, patch it, revisit if it causes a real incident. Manual certificate inventory. The SSL expiry postmortem produced an action item to audit all manual certificates by end of April. This was partially done: the staging and production wildcards moved to Certificate Manager, but three internal service certificates were never audited. This is exactly the kind of item that causes the same incident twice. Verdict: finish it, it is half a day of work. Retrieval quality. Unmeasured, as documented at length elsewhere. Now being addressed. Test coverage on the agent layer. The callback logic that prevents duplicate responses has one regression test. The multi-user isolation fix has none, despite being the most serious bug found this year. Verdict: add tests for the isolation boundary specifically, since a regression there is a security incident rather than a bug. Runbook rot. The game day exercise found two of six runbooks stale. They were fixed, but nothing prevents the same drift recurring. Verdict: schedule game days quarterly. Feature flag debt. The policy is now in place but three flags predate it and have no owner. Verdict: assign or remove them. Load test realism. The GA launch incident showed our load tests measured steady state while the failure lived in the ramp. Verdict: this is the highest-value item on this list, because it hid a real bug that then found us in production.

title: Post-GA Review Meeting
content: Review meeting four weeks after GA. Metrics. Signups exceeded the target by 30%. Activation, defined as connecting at least one data source, sits at 54%, below the 65% target. Churn is too early to measure meaningfully. The launch day latency incident did not appear to affect signup conversion in any measurable way. Product feedback themes. The dashboard redesign is well received and the filter panel specifically is mentioned unprompted. The natural language query feature, shipped as a beta, is used more than expected and generates more support questions than expected, mostly about why a particular question could not be answered. Notes search generates the most negative feedback of any feature, consistently described as unpredictable rather than bad, which matches the internal assessment that the problem is unmeasured rather than known-broken. Support load. Roughly 40 tickets per week, dominated by onboarding questions and by natural language query confusion. The briefing document given to support two days before launch was reported as useful but incomplete on the natural language query feature specifically, which was the newest thing and therefore the least documented. Decisions. Activation gap is the top priority, and the leading hypothesis is that the data source connection flow is too long. Retrieval quality work proceeds as planned since it now has external evidence, not only internal discomfort. Natural language query moves from beta to supported once the documentation gap is closed.

title: 1:1 with Ananya Das - July
content: First 1:1 with Ananya two weeks into the internship. She is working on the retrieval evaluation harness, which suits her background in retrieval-augmented generation directly. She raised a good methodological concern: generating evaluation questions from the notes with a language model and then evaluating retrieval with the same family of model risks measuring how well the model agrees with itself rather than how well retrieval works. Her suggestion is that generated labels be treated as candidates requiring human review, which is the right instinct. She also noticed the corpus is small enough that recall at five is close to meaningless when the corpus itself is only a handful of documents.

title: Citation Resolution Requirements
content: Requirements for how retrieval results become citations in agent responses. The agent currently returns note id, title, content, and similarity, and the model weaves these into prose. Once chunking exists, the retrieved unit is a chunk rather than a note, and a chunk id means nothing to a user. Requirement one: every retrieved chunk must resolve to its parent note id and title, which is what the user recognises. Requirement two: when multiple chunks from the same note are retrieved, they collapse into one citation rather than appearing as duplicates. Requirement three: the chunk text should be available to the model even though the citation names the note, because the chunk is the part that actually answers the question. Requirement four: deleting a note must delete its chunks, which is a foreign key with cascade rather than application logic.

title: Quarterly Game Day Schedule
content: Formalised the game day schedule after the runbook rot finding. Quarterly, half a day, rotating the scenario. Q3 scenario is database failover, which is the runbook that was most stale. Q4 is a region outage, which we cannot actually fix given no multi-region support but can at least confirm we detect and communicate correctly. Each game day produces a written report and any runbook found stale is fixed within the week, not added to a backlog.

title: Q4 Budget and Cost Trend
content: Q4 budget request with the full year cost trend. Quarterly cloud spend: 15,100, then 18,400, then 21,000 actual for Q3 against 21,000 projected, and 24,500 requested for Q4. The Q4 rise is entirely post-GA production traffic. Savings realised this year: 2,000 per quarter from the AlloyDB development shutdown schedule, 3,200 per year from dropping the load testing licence, and roughly 1,400 per quarter from the observability platform switch. Total realised saving is close to 12,000 annualised. New spend requested: an additional Cloud Run minimum instance allocation sized for launch-style traffic rather than steady state, which the GA incident showed we need.

title: Ananya Internship Final Review
content: End of internship review for Ananya Das. She delivered the retrieval evaluation harness including the labelled question set, the recall and MRR metrics, and a documented baseline. Her methodological caution about generated labels shaped how the whole piece of work was framed and was the most valuable thing she contributed, more than the code. She also identified that the corpus size made several metrics degenerate, which changed the scope of the work before time was wasted on it. Recommendation: extend a full-time offer for after her graduation.

title: GA Launch Retrospective
content: Retrospective on the GA launch as a whole, not only the incident. What went well. The date held from March through September without slipping, which has never happened here before. The communications plan executed cleanly. On-call worked exactly as designed under real pressure. The runbook that mattered was accurate because it had been tested. What did not. Capacity was sized for existing traffic rather than launch traffic, a mistake that in hindsight was predictable. Load testing measured the wrong shape of load. Support documentation for the newest feature was the thinnest, which is backwards. What surprised us. Activation came in below target while signups came in above, suggesting the marketing worked better than the onboarding. Notes search drew more negative feedback than any other feature despite receiving the least engineering attention this year, which is a lesson about where unmeasured quality hides.

title: Hybrid Search Consideration
content: Considered adding lexical search alongside vector search. Dense retrieval handles paraphrase well and rare exact terms badly. A user searching for a specific error string or a person's name is better served by lexical matching. Postgres full text search is available with no new infrastructure, and combining rankings with reciprocal rank fusion avoids needing to calibrate scores between the two systems. Not committing to this yet; it is a candidate for the reranking work rather than a separate project, and it should be measured against the same eval set as everything else.

title: TechCorp Renewal Conversation
content: Renewal conversation with TechCorp ahead of the annual date. Priya confirmed they are renewing and expanding by two seats. Their CTO cited the latency work and the directness during the Meridian-style multi-region conversation as reasons for trust. Feature requests for next year: the natural language query feature promoted out of beta, and better search over their own uploaded documents, which is the same retrieval quality problem in a different surface.

title: Next Year Planning - Early Draft
content: Early draft of next year's plan. Themes. First, retrieval and knowledge quality, now that it is measured and now that two customers have asked for document search. Second, activation, which is the clearest gap from the GA data. Third, multi-region, which has now appeared in two enterprise conversations and crossed the threshold set when Meridian was lost. Not themes: mobile, which still nobody asks for, and the older API service, which continues to be patched rather than owned.

title: Evaluation as a Standing Practice
content: Proposal to make evaluation a standing practice rather than a one-off project. The retrieval eval harness exists and has a committed baseline. The argument is that any system whose quality is subjective and whose changes are frequent deserves the same treatment: a labelled set, a metric, and a number committed to version control that later changes are measured against. Candidates beyond retrieval: the natural language query feature, where correctness of generated SQL is measurable against a labelled set, and the agent routing logic, where the correct sub-agent for a given request is a label. Both currently rely on someone trying it and forming an impression.

title: Retrieval Work Retrospective
content: Retrospective on the retrieval quality work specifically. What worked. Building the evaluation harness before changing anything was the correct order and was harder to argue for than it should have been, because it produces no visible improvement on its own. Having a committed baseline number made every subsequent conversation concrete. Reporting the null result honestly, where a change did not help, preserved trust in the numbers that did move. What was harder than expected. Labelling. Generated questions were phrased too much like the source notes and had to be rewritten to resemble how someone actually asks. Several labels were simply wrong and would have quietly corrupted the measurement if they had not been reviewed. What we would do differently. Size the corpus honestly at the start. Several metrics were degenerate on the original corpus and this was noticed only after the harness was built, which wasted effort that a five minute check would have saved.
